title: REPORT: Tsukuba's 1-GW AI power question — what the data-center buildout could really change for residents
summary: Goodman's Tsukuba Tech Central is real, large and directly relevant to Ibaraki: its first phase is 50 MW, while the master-planned campus has up to 1,000 MW of secured power capacity. That does not mean Tsukuba is consuming 1 GW today, and it does not prove Tokai Daini is being restarted for the project. The deeper issue is that AI and data centers are becoming large enough to change Japan's electricity-demand outlook, grid investment, water planning and the political economics of nuclear power.
why_it_matters: For Tsukuba and nearby residents, the practical questions are not whether AI servers use a lot of electricity—they do—but how fast the campus grows, what grid upgrades are required, who ultimately bears network costs, how cooling water is supplied, what local tax and infrastructure benefits are returned, and whether rising 24/7 demand strengthens the case for nuclear and other firm low-carbon generation. The local impact depends on these implementation choices, not on a sensational one-reactor comparison alone.

claims.text: Goodman lists Tsukuba Tech Central TYO05 as under construction, with a 50 MW first phase and up to 1,000 MW of power capacity upon full completion.
claims.basis: Goodman's current project and data-center portfolio pages.

claims.text: The 1,000 MW figure is secured or planned campus capacity, not evidence that the site is currently drawing 1,000 MW. Goodman's current portfolio lists 50 MW as leased at Tsukuba.
claims.basis: Goodman's own distinction between first-phase/leased capacity and power upon completion.

claims.text: Tsukuba City says the broader site was sold for ¥11,029,248,000 and is planned for data centers, logistics, disaster-resilience facilities and amenities.
claims.basis: Tsukuba City land-use and sale disclosure.

claims.text: OCCTO's 2026 outlook individually counts 7.62 GW of additional maximum demand from new data centers and semiconductor plants by FY2035, of which data centers account for 6.61 GW.

OCCTO projects 56.8 TWh of additional annual electricity demand from new data centers and semiconductor plants by FY2035, equal to 6.71% of projected national demand; data centers alone account for 49.4 TWh.

Japan's Seventh Strategic Energy Plan treats rising electricity demand associated with digitalization and data centers as part of the reason the country must expand reliable decarbonized electricity supply, with the 2040 outlook including nuclear at roughly 20% alongside a much larger renewable share.
claims.basis: Cabinet-approved national energy policy and 2040 outlook.

claims.text: Tokai Daini has a rated electric output of 1.10 GW, which makes the 1-GW Tsukuba campus a useful order-of-magnitude comparison if fully built, but Tokai Daini was producing 0 MW on September 6, 2026.
claims.basis: Japan Atomic Power Company plant specifications and live operating-status page.

claims.text: METI says AI-oriented data centers have higher server power density and heat output, increasing the importance of high-capacity cooling and potentially industrial-water demand as liquid cooling expands.
Ibaraki Prefecture passed the first screening in 2026 for the national GX Strategic Region program's data-center concentration category.
claims.basis: METI GX Strategic Region selection announcement.

claims.text: Japanese grid planners explicitly warn that simply reinforcing the network for each new large-load request can increase network costs and ultimately push up electricity charges, which is why government policy is trying to steer data centers toward locations with usable grid capacity and coordinated infrastructure.

AI and data-center growth strengthens the economic case for firm 24/7 generation, including nuclear, but the available public evidence does not show that Tokai Daini is being restarted specifically to power Goodman Tsukuba.
claims.basis: National demand and energy-policy evidence establish a broad connection; no project-specific power-supply contract linking TYO05 to Tokai Daini is publicly identified.

claims.text: The most credible household risk is indirect: inefficient or oversized grid expansion can flow through network charges over time. It would be inaccurate to claim that the Tsukuba project by itself will raise a household bill by a specific yen amount based on current public data.
claims.basis: Grid-cost policy documents explain the mechanism but do not publish a project-specific household tariff impact.

claims.text: The project's local economic value should be judged more by tax base, construction activity, infrastructure and associated technology investment than by expectations of factory-scale permanent employment, because hyperscale data centers are highly capital- and power-intensive rather than labor-intensive once operational.
claims.basis: Project scale and public development goals; no claim is made about an unpublished permanent headcount.

editorial_visual.scene: a realistic editorial illustration of a huge modern AI data-center campus on the Tsukuba plain at dusk, high-voltage transmission lines and substations feeding rows of data halls, with the distant silhouette of a coastal nuclear power station used only as a visual comparison; homes and a family in the foreground looking at an electricity bill and city map; cooling infrastructure and water pipes subtly visible; serious Japanese news-magazine style, no logos, no text, no apocalyptic imagery
editorial_visual.caption: The real AI-energy story is the infrastructure between the server rack and the household power bill

content.key_message: Tsukuba is becoming part of Japan's AI power infrastructure. The 1-GW headline is real as an eventual secured-capacity figure, but the immediate project is 50 MW. The consequence residents should watch is not a mythical private nuclear reactor for AI; it is the cumulative effect of large 24/7 loads on substations, transmission investment, water planning, generation policy and local public benefits.
content.report_scope: Tsukuba AI/data-center development, electricity demand, household cost exposure, water, local benefits and the Tokai Daini nuclear connection
executive_summary: Goodman TYO05 in Tsukuba is under construction. Its first phase is 50 MW, while the master plan allows up to 1,000 MW of secured power capacity. Do not confuse the eventual ceiling with today's consumption.

A fully built 1-GW campus would be in roughly the same power-output class as Tokai Daini's 1.10-GW rated capacity. That is useful for understanding scale, but it is not evidence that the nuclear plant will supply the campus directly.
The national effect is already measurable. OCCTO expects new data centers alone to add 6.61 GW of maximum demand and 49.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption by FY2035.

Japan's energy strategy now explicitly plans around electricity-demand growth linked to digitalization and data centers. This strengthens policy support for both renewable expansion and nuclear utilization rather than proving a one-to-one AI-to-nuclear relationship.

Grid cost is the household issue to watch. Official planners warn that repeated network reinforcement for large new loads can raise network costs and ultimately electricity charges if development is poorly coordinated.

Water is a real engineering issue, especially for high-density AI servers and liquid cooling, but no reliable public project-specific figure currently justifies claiming a certain number of liters per day for TYO05.

Tsukuba should measure the bargain: tax revenue, disaster-resilience infrastructure, construction and technology investment versus land use, utility demand, noise/heat concerns and any public share of infrastructure costs.

the_scale_without_hype.correct_interpretation: The numbers are comparable as power capacity, not as proof of a dedicated supply relationship. A data center is a load and a nuclear station is a generator; actual annual energy use also depends on how fully the campus is built and utilized.

what_residents_may_actually_feel.assessment: Possible indirect pressure, not a proven Tsukuba surcharge
what_residents_may_actually_feel.detail: Transmission and substation expansion is recovered through the electricity system under regulated cost-allocation rules. National planners are changing siting and connection rules precisely because inefficient large-load connections can increase network costs. There is currently no defensible project-specific estimate such as 'your bill will rise ¥X'.

A campus capable of scaling from tens to hundreds of megawatts requires long-term utility coordination. This can mean new substations, high-voltage equipment, transmission reinforcement and construction corridors. The timing and cost allocation matter as much as the total megawatts.

what_residents_may_actually_feel.assessment: Real concern, project-specific magnitude still unknown
what_residents_may_actually_feel.detail: AI servers produce much higher heat density than conventional computing. Japan is already planning for higher water demand from liquid-cooled data centers. TYO05 says water is secured, but public material reviewed for this report does not provide a reliable daily-consumption number or detailed cooling-water balance.

what_residents_may_actually_feel.assessment: Strong during construction; permanent headcount should not be exaggerated
what_residents_may_actually_feel.detail: Data centers create major engineering, civil, electrical and maintenance work, but they do not employ people at the same density as large manufacturing plants. Local value should therefore also be measured through taxes, supplier work, infrastructure and associated digital-industry attraction.

The site itself involved an approximately ¥11.03-billion land sale. The long-term public bargain should include fixed-asset and other tax effects, disaster-resilience facilities and whether the development brings useful infrastructure that serves more than the campus.

Large data centers reject substantial heat and use fans, pumps, chillers and backup equipment. The actual neighborhood impact depends on equipment placement, cooling design, acoustic treatment and operating conditions; generic internet estimates should not be substituted for TYO05-specific environmental data.

what_residents_may_actually_feel.assessment: Indirect policy connection is real; direct Tokai-Daini link is unproven
what_residents_may_actually_feel.detail: Large constant loads improve the economic value of dependable low-carbon generation. Japan's energy plan is responding to rising electricity demand by pushing both renewables and nuclear. But there is no public evidence identified here of a dedicated TYO05-Tokai Daini supply agreement or a restart decision made specifically for this campus.

national_context: OCCTO expects new data centers and semiconductor plants to add 7.62 GW of maximum demand by FY2035. Data centers account for 6.61 GW of that total.
The same projects are expected to add 56.8 TWh of annual electricity demand by FY2035, about 6.71% of projected national consumption. Data centers account for 49.4 TWh.
This is large enough to alter a national demand trajectory that had previously been shaped strongly by population decline and efficiency improvements.

METI is therefore promoting 'Watt-Bit' coordination: planning electricity networks and digital infrastructure together instead of approving large data-center clusters first and fixing the grid afterward.

Ibaraki's selection as a promising data-center-concentration region under the GX Strategic Region process suggests that TYO05 may be part of a broader regional infrastructure strategy rather than an isolated facility.

true: Tokai Daini is rated at 1.10 GW, close to the eventual 1-GW power capacity advertised for the full Tsukuba campus.
Japan expects AI, data centers and other electrification to raise future electricity demand.
National policy is seeking greater use of firm decarbonized generation, including nuclear, alongside major renewable expansion.
A large 24/7 industrial load can improve the economics of power-system assets that provide dependable generation and grid capacity.
not_proven: That the full 1-GW Tsukuba campus will definitely be built out or continuously draw 1 GW.
That Tokai Daini is being restarted specifically because of Goodman TYO05.
That electricity generated at Tokai Daini would be physically or contractually dedicated to the Tsukuba campus.
That the project will cause a quantifiable household electricity-price increase based on currently public project data.

questions_tsukuba_should_get_answered: What is the expected power ramp by year after the first 50-MW phase—not just the eventual 1,000-MW ceiling?
Which transmission and substation projects are required specifically because of this campus, and what is the cost allocation between the developer, grid operator and general network users?
What cooling architecture will each data-center phase use, and what are expected peak and annual water withdrawals and consumption?
What renewable, nuclear, thermal or contracted clean-power arrangements will support the campus's annual electricity use?
What are the expected permanent local jobs after construction is complete?
What fixed-asset tax and other recurring municipal revenue is expected at 50 MW, 100 MW, 500 MW and full buildout?
What noise, backup-generator, heat-rejection and emergency-fuel standards apply at the nearest residential boundaries?
What parts of the new power, fibre, roads, water or disaster-resilience infrastructure provide a benefit to residents outside the data-center site?
content.bottom_line_for_households: Do not panic over the phrase 'one nuclear reactor of AI.' The first live scale is far smaller than 1 GW, and a dedicated nuclear link is not established. But do not dismiss the project either. Japan's official forecasts show that data-center growth is now large enough to affect national electricity planning. For residents, the most important scrutiny is financial and infrastructural: how much new grid and water capacity is built, how those costs are allocated, and whether Tsukuba receives enough lasting public value in return.
evidence_for: Goodman itself publishes the 50-MW first phase and 1,000-MW eventual capacity, confirming that the scale is not media speculation.
OCCTO's official FY2035 forecast shows data centers becoming a multi-gigawatt national load category.
Japan's strategic energy and Watt-Bit policies explicitly respond to electricity-demand growth from digital infrastructure.
METI is already considering water availability, large-load siting and coordinated grid investment as data-center policy issues.
Ibaraki is already inside the government's emerging data-center concentration strategy.
evidence_against: The 1-GW figure describes eventual secured capacity rather than current consumption or a committed immediate buildout.
The first phase is only 50 MW, so using 1 GW as today's local load would exaggerate the present impact by roughly twenty times.
There is no public evidence identified in this review that links Tokai Daini restart authorization directly to TYO05.
Project-specific water use, household tariff impact, permanent employment and final generation mix remain insufficiently disclosed for precise numerical claims.
content.connection: The important chain is AI demand -> more hyperscale data centers -> larger 24/7 electricity loads -> pressure for grid capacity and dependable generation -> stronger policy case for renewables, storage, thermal flexibility and nuclear -> possible network-cost and land/water tradeoffs at the local level. The link is systemic, not a simple wire running from one nuclear plant to one AI building.
content.alternative_explanation: Some of the electricity-demand increase often attributed to 'AI' is actually broader cloud computing, digital services and conventional data-center expansion. Semiconductor factories and wider electrification also raise demand. Therefore nuclear and grid policy should not be presented as an AI-only response.
watch_next: Goodman announcements on additional TYO05 phases beyond the first 50 MW
Identity and workload profile of additional hyperscale tenants
TEPCO-area transmission/substation plans connected to the Tsukuba load cluster
GX Strategic Region final designation and Ibaraki implementation plan
Tokai Daini safety-work completion, local consent and restart decisions
Any project-specific renewable or long-term power-purchase agreements
Tsukuba disclosures on expected recurring tax revenue and permanent employment
content.what_would_change_mind: The assessment would become substantially more serious if Goodman commits several hundred additional megawatts on a firm construction schedule, if the grid operator identifies major TYO05-driven transmission investments recoverable broadly from customers, or if project-specific water use proves large relative to local supply. Conversely, a slow buildout, developer-funded dedicated infrastructure, low-water cooling and strong local tax/public-benefit arrangements would reduce the household-impact concern.
content.implications: Tsukuba should treat data centers like other major infrastructure-intensive industries: welcome investment, but demand transparent accounting of utility use, network costs, tax benefits, environmental controls and community return. Nationally, AI is becoming one factor that makes Japan's old assumption of steadily falling electricity demand less reliable and makes the nuclear-renewables-grid debate materially more urgent.
content.history: Japan spent much of the post-Fukushima period planning around weak or declining electricity demand while simultaneously reducing nuclear utilization. The rapid rise of cloud computing, generative AI, semiconductor investment and electrification is now forcing planners to revisit that assumption. Tsukuba's planned campus is a local example of that national transition.
